nameStory: This moth gets its "white-dotted" name from the two distinctive small silver spots that shine like tiny beacons on each forewing. The "prominent" part of its name comes from the pointed tuft of scales that sticks up between its wings on its back, making it look like it's wearing a little mohawk hairdo!
description: The White-dotted Prominent is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan of about 2 inches that you might spot fluttering around outdoor lights on warm summer evenings. Its wings are dressed in warm tan or dull orange colors, decorated with those telltale silver spots that catch the light. Like all prominent moths, it has a fuzzy, robust body and that characteristic pointed tuft of scales on its back that makes it easy to distinguish from other moth families.

idTips.label: Silver wing spots
idTips.description: Look for two small, bright silver spots on each forewing that shimmer like tiny mirrors when light hits them at the right angle

idTips.label: Pointed back tuft
idTips.description: A distinctive spike of fuzzy scales projects upward from the thorax between the wings, feeling stiff to the touch if you gently examine a resting moth

idTips.label: Wing color
idTips.description: Wings are warm tan to dull orange-brown, with a soft, velvety texture that feels like fine suede when touched gently

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About 2 inches across with a sturdy, triangular silhouette when at rest, wings held tent-like over a robust, fuzzy body

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Active shortly after dusk, attracted to porch lights and outdoor fixtures, with a somewhat heavy, direct flight pattern

habitat: You'll find White-dotted Prominents in New England's deciduous forests, especially at higher elevations where maples, oaks, and birches dominate the canopy. They prefer mature woodland areas with diverse tree species rather than young forests or forest edges. Look for them around outdoor lights near forested areas during their active season.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring as temperatures warm, becoming active around porch lights and outdoor fixtures after dusk.
seasonality.summer: Peak adult activity occurs through early summer when mating and egg-laying take place. This is the best time to spot them at lights.
seasonality.fall: Adults have finished their life cycle, but caterpillars are actively feeding on deciduous trees before pupating for winter.
seasonality.winter: Moths are dormant as pupae in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger their emergence as adults.

funFact: White-dotted Prominents are early risers in the moth world - they start flying shortly after sunset but head back to their hiding spots well before dawn, almost like they have a strict bedtime curfew while most other moths party all night long!
confusionNotes: The silver wing spots are your best bet for identification - many other brown moths lack these distinctive metallic markings. If you're unsure, look for that pointed tuft on the back, which separates prominent moths from most other moth families.
contextualKnowledge: This species goes by several common names including "rough prominent" and "tawny prominent," so don't be confused if you see it listed differently in field guides - they're all the same moth! The varying names reflect regional preferences and the moth's somewhat variable coloration.
compareHints: Since this is the only Nadata species commonly found in New England, compare it with other prominent moths in the region. Most other prominents lack the distinctive silver spots and have different colored wing patterns, making the White-dotted Prominent relatively easy to distinguish within its family by those metallic markings alone.
